## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

# neatlogs — facts sheet

Source: https://neatlogs.com (homepage and pricing, read 2026-10-11). Only facts stated there.

## What it is
- Tagline: "The fastest path from failure to fix."
- neatlogs finds what's failing in AI agent runs, works out why, and hands you a fix.
- Built for teams shipping agents.

## Features
- Traces & Detections: see every production run and the failures hiding inside them.
- Investigations: evidence, root cause, and a fix brief a coding agent can ship.
- Evals: describe what good looks like and score every run against it.
- Collaboration: support, product and engineering work from the same evidence.
- Ask @neatlogs questions in Slack, the app, or Linear.
- Investigate from the terminal via the CLI or MCP.
- SDKs for Python, TypeScript and Go.

## Pricing
- Free: $0 forever — 100k spans/month, 3 investigations/month, 5 detectors, 2 users, 1 project, 14-day retention.
- Starter: $99/month ($84/month billed annually) — 250k spans/month, 50 investigations/month, unlimited users, 5 projects, 30-day retention.
- Pro: $499/month ($424/month billed annually) — 1M spans/month, unlimited investigations and evaluations, audit log and SSO, 90-day retention.
- Enterprise: custom annual pricing — SAML/SCIM, data residency, VPC or self-hosted ingest, SLA.
- Starter and Pro: first month free.

## Links
- Start free: https://app.neatlogs.com
- Docs: https://docs.neatlogs.com
# Entire — facts sheet

Sources: https://entire.io (homepage, read 2026-10-11); https://github.com/entireio/cli. Only facts stated there.

## What it is
- Tagline: "Every agent session stored in your repo."
- Git hosting platform and CLI that stores each agent session, prompt and tool call alongside your commits.
- Founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke (launched February 2026).

## Features
- A checkpoint for every commit, linking the code change to the agent session that produced it.
- Sessions sync with commits: conversations are captured and linked to git history automatically.
- Private by design: secrets are detected and redacted before anything is stored.
- Send a branch to multiple agents in parallel for review.
- Search both code changes and the sessions that explain them.
- Resume work across agents with session state carried forward.
- Host code in-region: India, Australia, EU and US.
- One command creates a regional mirror of a GitHub repo.
- Works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Pi, OpenCode, Droid, Antigravity and Amp.
- The CLI is open source (MIT licensed).

## Pricing
- No prices are published on the homepage. The CLI is free and open source.

## Links
- Get started: https://entire.io/login
- Install: curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

Here are 5 ideas. Each one has a part for all three tools, and they're ranked for this hackathon. Your scoring weights are autonomy 30%, sponsor tools 25%, demo 20%, building in public 15%, usefulness 10%. The deadline is **tonight at 11:55 PM IST**.

**What each tool does:**
- **neatlogs** traces agent runs, spots failures, finds the root cause and writes a fix brief for a coding agent.
- **Entire** saves every coding-agent session next to the commit it produced, so each change carries its "why".
- **cfo.ai** (Runway Financial's new name, launched Sept 2026) has an AI CFO called "Ari". Ari tracks revenue, cash flow, churn and margins, warns you about problems, and does forecasts. It connects to Stripe, QuickBooks, NetSuite, Salesforce and Snowflake. I found no public API, so assume you feed it through Stripe or an export.

Together they form a loop: **cfo.ai finds the money problem → neatlogs finds why → a coding agent fixes it → Entire records the fix.** The best ideas use that whole loop.

---

### 1. A business that fixes itself (AutoShelf v2) ⭐ recommended
Your agents run the store. Ari flags a drop, for example "margin fell 30%". neatlogs traces it to a cause, say the Support agent giving refunds too freely. Its fix brief goes to Claude Code, which patches the prompt or guardrail. Entire saves that session with the commit, and the next run shows the margin recovering.
- **Why it wins:** it shows the most autonomy (agents run the business *and* fix it) and uses all three tools for real.
- **Effort:** low. You already have the agents, neatlogs tracing, `export_cfo.ts` and the fault injection in `src/sim/inject.ts`.

### 2. "Is this agent worth its salary?" (agent cost vs. value)
Turn neatlogs token and cost data from each run into unit economics in cfo.ai: inference cost per order and ROI per agent. Entire links each prompt change to its cost change, e.g. "commit a1b2 made Support 40% cheaper and it kept the same eval score."
- **Strong on:** usefulness and a clear demo. **Weaker on:** autonomy, since it mostly reports rather than acts.

### 3. Prompt CI with a money gate
Every prompt or agent change committed through Entire triggers a neatlogs eval run on fixed test cases. A cfo.ai forecast then projects the monthly cost at scale. The merge is blocked if quality drops or cost goes over budget.
- **Strong on:** usefulness for developers and a clean before/after demo. **Effort:** medium.

### 4. Agent incident postmortem, priced in dollars
When an agent fails in production, neatlogs finds the root cause. Entire's session search finds which commit and *which agent session* introduced the bug (git blame for prompts). cfo.ai puts a number on the damage: "$X revenue lost, here's the fix."
- **Strong on:** a good story for posts. **Weaker on:** autonomy, unless the bot also opens the fix PR.

### 5. What did this feature cost to build with AI?
Entire captures the coding-agent sessions behind each feature, neatlogs traces them, and cfo.ai treats AI coding spend like payroll, with budget, burn and cost per feature shipped.
- **Risk:** I haven't checked whether Entire sessions include token or cost data. It's also the furthest from your current code.

---

**My pick: #1.** It reuses about 80% of what you've built, and it's the only idea that scores high on autonomy, which is the biggest weight. You can add #2's cost-per-agent view on the cfo.ai side for little extra work. Do this first: put the neatlogs credentials in `.env` and do one real run with a failure injected, so you have a real trace to show.

Two things to check before you commit:
- **cfo.ai access:** find out whether the hackathon gives you access, and whether data goes in through Stripe test mode or a sheet. If it's Stripe, #1 needs the store's sales to go through Stripe test mode.
- **Leftover swarm files:** they're half-built and break the TypeScript build (`src/swarm/engine.ts` imports a missing file). Delete them or leave them out before you build anything.

- [SiliconANGLE: Runway rebrands as cfo.ai, launches Ari](https://siliconangle.com/?p=837986)
- [CrewAI docs: neatlogs integration](https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.21/en/observability/neatlogs.md)

# neatHack: AI Agent Hackathon

**Overview:** A 48-hour online hackathon run by neatlogs, October 10–12, 2026. Teams or solo builders create an AI agent that completes a substantial task from start to finish. The page's headline goal is agents you'd "trust to run without you watching."

## Key Dates (IST)
- **Oct 10:** Kickoff call at 9:00 AM, with a workshop from TheVibeFounder and a Q&A. Hacking begins at 12:30 PM.
- **Oct 11:** Final workshops and office hours.
- **Oct 12:** Submissions open at 7:00 PM and have a planned close of 11:55 PM. The final cutoff is announced on Discord.
- **Oct 16:** Winners announced.

## Track
There is one track: build an agent, or a team of agents, that completes a substantial task. Judging focuses on eight areas:
- Planning
- Tool use
- State
- Context
- Execution
- Recovery
- Verification
- Iteration

**Example tasks** (illustrative only, not required):
- Investigate and fix a GitHub issue
- Answer a research question with cited sources
- Monitor a running system and fix problems it finds
- Coordinate several agents that combine their results
- Keep working on a long task while the environment changes

## Required Sponsor Tools
Projects must use all three:

- **neatlogs:** Trace every agent run (model and tool calls, state changes, retries, failures, latency, tokens, cost) and use the traces to build and improve the agent. Traces should help you find the code behind failures and compare runs.
- **Entire:** Give your coding agent repository context using Checkpoints (saved context behind each change) and entire-graph (repository relationships).
- **cfo.ai:** Plan the agent's pricing, costs, revenue, and runway. The business plan must be included in your submission. Sign-up requires a card. Cancel the subscription immediately in Settings → Billing to avoid being charged. The team provides credits directly.

## Judging Criteria
| Category | Weight |
|---|---|
| The agent (handles a substantial task end to end) | 30% |
| Use of neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai | 25% |
| Demo video (clarity of the agent and tool use) | 20% |
| Building in public | 15% |
| Usefulness and originality | 10% |

## Submission Requirements
Back up claims with evidence judges can check:
- **Agent improvement:** Before-and-after runs (e.g., two neatlogs traces) with compared numbers
- **neatlogs use:** Trace links or screenshots
- **Entire use:** Checkpoints or entire-graph output from your repo
- **cfo.ai use:** Business plan covering pricing, costs, revenue, and runway
- **Failure recovery:** A run where an action failed and the agent's next steps are visible
- **Building in public:** Links to posts tagged #neatHack
- **Original work:** A public repo with commits dated during the hackathon
- **Demo video**

**How to submit:** Quote the official neatlogs post with your team name, project name, public repo, and demo. neatlogs and cfo.ai will engage with the first 50 quote tweets.

## Prizes ($19,000 total including credits)
**Cash and partner credits:**
- **1st:** $2,000 cash + $5,000 Dodo Payments credits
- **2nd:** $1,000 cash + $3,000 Dodo Payments credits
- **3rd:** $500 cash + $1,000 Dodo Payments credits
- **Community winner:** $500 cash, for community impact. Can be won alongside a top-three placement.

Each top-three winner also gets 3 months of neatlogs Pro (valued at $1,500).

**Building resources:**
- **LiteLLM:** One $20 model budget per team or solo builder, for Nova and Claude models through an OpenAI-compatible API
- **AWS:** One $25 allowance per team or solo builder (EC2, Lambda, IAM, load balancers; Bedrock not included). Available to the first 350 teams to complete web check-in.
- **Crustdata:** 5,000 credits for every participant (company and people data APIs)

## Sponsors and Partners
cfo.ai, Entire, Dodo Payments, AWS, TheVibeFounder, Crustdata, and Orchestrator.inc.

## Judges and Mentors
- **Judges:** Haimantika Mitra (Entire), Abhi Singh (Entire), Prateek Karnal (Orchestrator.inc), Ajay Yadav (neatlogs), and Akshay Hangloo (neatlogs)
- **Mentors:** Karan Pargal, Rohan Mukherjee, Chetan Raj, Ankush Dharkar, and Rithvik K

## Getting Started
1. Register on Luma.
2. Join the Discord.
3. Complete web check-in and confirm your team.
4. Submit your project during the October 12 window.

**Note:** The page's FAQ lists questions on team formation, conduct rules, and pre-event building, but the answers are not included in the content provided, so I can't summarize them. Check the FAQ on the page or the Discord for those details.

content.text:
The official page changes my earlier list. I had two of the three tools wrong:

- **cfo.ai** isn't something your agent feeds data into. You use it to write a **business plan for your agent**: pricing, costs, revenue and runway. That plan is a required part of the submission.
- **Entire** is for giving **your coding agent** context about the repo, through Checkpoints and entire-graph. It doesn't have to be part of the product at all.
- **Judging:** there's one track, "an agent that does a substantial task end to end." It's scored on planning, tool use, state, context, execution, recovery, verification and iteration.
- **Evidence you must show:** two neatlogs traces compared before and after, a run where something failed and the agent recovered, Entire checkpoints, the cfo.ai plan, posts tagged #neatHack, and a public repo with commits dated during the event.
- **Judges:** they're from Entire, neatlogs and Orchestrator.inc.

I saved these rules to project memory.

## Revised ideas

### 1. Trace-to-fix agent (fixes another agent's failures) ⭐
This is close to neatlogs' own pitch, "failure to fix," and it uses Entire for real. Your AutoShelf agents are the "patient": a fault is injected and they fail. The Fixer agent then:
1. pulls the failing trace from neatlogs;
2. finds the code behind it using the Entire checkpoint for that change;
3. writes a patch;
4. reruns the same seed to check the fix;
5. retries if the check fails.

- **Built-in proof:** before and after traces, a recovery run and Entire checkpoints come out of the agent's normal work.
- **cfo.ai plan:** sell it as a dev tool, priced per fix or per seat, with LLM cost per fix as the main cost.
- **Effort:** medium. AutoShelf, the tracing and the fault injection already exist; the new part is the Fixer loop.

### 2. AutoShelf as it is: a self-running store operator
The agents run the store, use guardrails to check actions before taking them, and recover from injected faults like a bad refund or an API down.
- **Fits:** the example task "monitor a running system and fix problems it finds."
- **cfo.ai plan:** a SaaS for small sellers.
- **Effort:** lowest. This is the safe choice if time gets short.

### 3. Prospect research agent (Crustdata, cited sources)
Given a product, it finds matching companies and people through Crustdata, checks each claim against a source, and writes outreach with citations.
- **Recovery:** it handles rate limits and empty results.
- **cfo.ai plan:** price per qualified lead.
- **Reuse:** you already have the Crustdata tools, and every participant gets 5k credits.

### 4. Payment reconciliation agent (Dodo Payments)
It watches test-mode payments, catches failed webhooks, refunds and mismatches, fixes the ledger, and confirms it balances.
- **Fit:** good for "state" and "verification," and Dodo is the prize sponsor.
- **Effort:** a newer build.

### 5. Repo maintenance agent
It reads a GitHub issue, uses Entire's graph and checkpoints to understand the code, fixes the issue, runs the tests, and opens a PR.
- **Fit:** it's the page's first example task, so it's well aligned.
- **Downside:** many teams will build this, so it scores low on originality.

## Recommendation
**#1, built on top of #2.** AutoShelf becomes the patient and the Fixer is the new agent. If the Fixer isn't stable by about 6 PM IST, fall back to plain #2. Submissions open at 7 PM.

Start the slow items now, whichever idea you pick:
- **cfo.ai:** sign up and cancel straight away in Settings → Billing. Write the plan with numbers from a real run.
- **Entire:** run `entire` in this repo so your checkpoints start getting recorded.
- **Repo:** make it public and commit the work that's still uncommitted.
- **Posts:** put up at least one #neatHack post today.

### 2. Startup due-diligence memo agent
Give it a company name. It pulls headcount, funding and hiring trends from Crustdata and the web, writes an investor memo, and checks each number against two sources. When sources disagree, it flags the contradiction.

- **Business:** priced per memo for angel investors and small VC firms.
- **Effort:** low, since you already have the Crustdata code and 5k free credits.

### 3. Spreadsheet model auditor
Give it a financial `.xlsx`. It finds broken formulas, hardcoded numbers and wrong cell ranges, fixes them, and recomputes to prove the totals now reconcile.
- **Demo:** your `freelancer-budget-tracker.xlsx` with bugs planted in it.
- **Business:** it fits cfo.ai's finance theme well.

### 4. Docs drift fixer
It runs every code snippet in a project's README and docs, finds the ones that no longer work, works out what changed in the code, rewrites the docs, and reruns the snippets until they pass.
- **Entire:** the checkpoints explain *why* the code changed, which is a natural use.

### 5. Tender and grant application agent
It finds an open grant or tender, pulls out the eligibility rules and required sections, drafts each section, and checks the draft against every rule before putting the package together.
- **Recovery:** when a requirement is missing, it goes back and fetches it or asks you.

**My pick: #1.** It's the most original and aimed straight at these judges. It also produces the evidence the rules ask for (before and after traces, a failure-recovery run) through its normal work. Submissions close tonight, so #2 is the faster, safer fallback.

content.text:
Here are 8 more ideas, none repeating the earlier ones.

1. **Bug reproduction agent.** It takes a vague bug report ("checkout breaks sometimes") and writes a test that reproduces it. It counts as done only when the test fails on the current code. It doesn't fix anything; it proves the bug is real. Recovery: when a guess doesn't reproduce the bug, it narrows down and tries again.

2. **Accessibility fixer.** It crawls a site, runs accessibility checks (axe), fixes the HTML and CSS in the repo, and runs the checks again. You get clear before and after numbers, e.g. "42 violations → 3", which fits the required before/after evidence.

3. **Fresh-machine setup agent.** It launches a clean EC2 box (you have $25 AWS credit) and follows the repo's README to get the app running. It logs every step that breaks, fixes it, and outputs a setup script that works first time. It's done only when the app answers a health check.

4. **Self-repairing scraper / website-to-API.** Point it at a site with no API and it builds a typed API on top of it. When the site's layout changes and the scraper breaks, it notices and rebuilds it. This fits the hackathon's example task "keep working while the environment changes."

5. **Cloud cost janitor.** It scans an AWS account for idle or forgotten resources, prices each one, does a dry run, then shuts them down and checks the bill impact. It fits cfo.ai's theme well, since savings are the pitch.

6. **API fuzzer.** It reads an OpenAPI spec, generates edge-case requests, finds the ones that crash or return wrong data, and reduces each to the smallest request that still fails. It then writes the bug report.

7. **Messy-CSV-to-database agent.** It takes a data dump, works out the columns and types, cleans the data, writes checks, and loads it into a database. Rows that fail go into a quarantine table with reasons, and it finishes with a report.

8. **Meeting-to-tickets agent.** It takes a call transcript, pulls out the tasks, removes ones already filed in GitHub issues, assigns owners, and checks that nothing from the transcript was missed.

**Best for tonight:**
- **#2 (accessibility fixer):** the easiest numbers to show before and after.
- **#1 (bug reproduction):** the most original.
- **#4 (self-repairing scraper):** the strongest recovery story for the demo.

All three are small enough to build before submissions close tonight.

lines: -You are one agent in a swarm: a small group of peers working on one goal together. There is no manager. Nobody will tell you what to do except the plan the swarm agrees on.
-- Work happens in **rounds**. In each round you work on your own for a few steps, then the swarm syncs on the shared **message board**.
-- You have your own **memory** for this run (`save_memory`). Others can't see it. Use it for things you'll need in later rounds: partial results, what you tried, what failed.
-- The **board** is how the swarm thinks together. Post only what others need: key findings, results with how you got them, open questions, and what you think should happen next. No chatter.
-- Between rounds everyone proposes a next step and votes. The winning plan gives each agent an assignment. Do your assignment first.
-- Bring your **angle** (below). Different angles are why a swarm beats one agent.
-- Don't duplicate work another agent already posted. Build on it, check it, or take a different route.
-- **Verify before you claim.** If you can compute or check something with a tool, do it. Say *how* you know: "computed with run_code", "from <url>", "reasoned, not checked".
-- If you find a mistake in someone's finding, post a correction with the evidence. Being right matters more than agreeing.
-- Be brief. Every token you use comes out of the swarm's shared budget.
-1. Read your assignment, your memory and the board.
-2. Do the work with your tools (a few steps at most).
-4. `post_to_board` 1–3 posts: findings (with evidence) or questions. If you have a candidate final answer, post it as a finding and say how confident you are.

**The number that drove everything: 0 leads, 62 visits, 4 page views, 10 posts of which 8 are unpublished with 0 tracked traffic.**

Analytics was explicit that n=4 makes any click-through conclusion noise. Cost: ~5.4k tokens.
2. **Analytics — competitor positioning.** Funded rivals (LangSmith $160M, Arize $131M, Braintrust $121M) all speak **engineer-first**. neatlogs' only uncrowded flank is the **non-engineer who owns correctness** — support lead, ops manager, finance reviewer. That's the one axis where an 11-person team is ahead, not behind. Cost: ~7.8k tokens.
3. **Content — listing + distribution + blog, briefed with that angle.** Cost: 10.4k of its 15k grant. **What I found (the number that drove everything):** neatlogs has **0 leads** — but it is *not* a conversion problem yet. Analytics: **62 storefront visits → 4 neatlogs listing views → 0 CTA clicks**, with **all 62 visits tagged `direct`**, and **all 10 posts at 0 visits / 0 leads**. Four ready neatlogs X posts are still sitting in **draft**. So the real problem is **distribution + measurement**, and n=4 is too small to say anything about the CTA. Analytics was explicit that redesigning the CTA now would be guessing.

**Actions taken (3):**
1. **Analytics — funnel/source diagnosis.** 62 visits, 0 attributed, 4 listing views, 0 leads, 10 posts with 0 visits. This is why I did *not* spend an action on listing copy: the listing is accurate and on-angle already; nobody has seen it.
2. **Analytics — competitor positioning angle (Langfuse / LangSmith / Braintrust).** Spent tokens, **returned an empty answer**. I did not re-ask and I did not let Content invent head-to-head claims as a substitute.

No UTMs added; still no live distribution.

**Also checked:** 0 open tickets, so Support had nothing to do — no waiting people were skipped.

**Honest state:** nothing changed on the storefront today. The 4 X drafts are still drafts and traffic is still unattributed.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text:
I fixed every problem in your trace, and the agents no longer fail silently. They still aren't shipping posts, though, for a reason you can fix in one command (see the end). All 54 tests pass and the build is clean; each fix had a failing test first, using the real token numbers from your traces.

**What I fixed:**

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Fixed token shares left 18.7k unspent while helpers were cut off | Each job now gets a grant from the unspent tokens, with a reserve kept for the Operator. A job too small to finish is refused before it starts. |
| The Operator guessed grant sizes too small | Grant sizes now come only from the rules. |
| Helpers stopped mid-sentence ("Stopped early") | When the budget can't cover another turn, that turn is the last: no tools, and the agent reports what's done and what isn't. |
| Content passed an empty answer up to the Operator (your trace) | An empty or cut-off reply is retried once. If that's empty too, the agent says it was cut off instead of returning nothing. |
| `mark_claims` crashed with "verdicts is not iterable" | Tools now check required inputs and tell the model which one is missing. |
| Analytics read posts for retired products on every call | Those posts are filtered out. |
| Your :3000 server was running last night's code | Restarted; your trace `e77bde38` came from the old code. |
| Redundant tools | Removed `set_price`, `refund_order` and `get_ai_spend`. A test now fixes each agent's exact tool list, so they can't come back unnoticed. |

**Before and after on real runs:**

| | Before (`a47c429e`) | After (`44e3802c`) |
|---|---|---|
| Agents stopped mid-sentence | 2 | 0 |
| Empty answers or crashed tools | yes | 0 |
| Jobs refused cleanly before starting | n/a | 1 ("NOT RUN: only 3799 free, needs 6000") |
| Every agent reports what's done and what isn't | no | yes |

**Two things still block shipping:**
1. **Your approval.** The Operator keeps asking Content to publish 4 X drafts, but publishing to X needs you. Content has no tool for it, so that job can't succeed. Look at the drafts and run `pnpm approve:all` if they're fine.
2. **Content thinks too long.** One turn is mostly reasoning, which uses up the turn before it acts. The fix is to lower Content's reasoning effort or split its job into smaller ones, again with a test first.

Nothing is committed yet. Next on the plan are Entire (`! curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`), a public repo with the commits, and the cfo.ai plan. Shall I commit this work and take on the Content fix?

done|## What the numbers show

Everything here rests on a **tiny sample** — 4 product-page views and 7 posts — so treat the rates as directional, not proven.

**Leads & spend (store, all products):**
- neatlogs: **0 leads**, **4 page visits**, 0 orders, $0.00 revenue
- Store totals: revenue **$19.00**, fees **–$1.90**, **AI/inference cost –$1.35**, profit **$15.75**
- So the AI spend has been **$1.35 total** — trivial, and more than covered by the $15.75 profit. Cost is not the problem. (Note: the $19.00 revenue is not attributed to neatlogs in the per-product breakdown — worth confirming where it came from.)

**Traffic sources:**
- **direct: 62 visits, 0 leads** — that's 100% of real storefront visits
- **simulated (paid): empty** — no campaigns running
- Every other channel (x, blog, referrer): **0 visits**

**Posts:**
- 7 posts total → **0 visits and 0 leads, every single one**
- 3 are **published blog** posts (e.g. "How to debug a failing AI agent: traces, failure detection, evals")
- 4 are **draft X posts — not live**, so they cannot bring traffic by definition

**The funnel, step by step:**
| Step | Count | Drop |
|---|---|---|
| Source visits (all direct) | 62 | — |
| neatlogs listing page views | 4 | 58 lost (93.5%) |
| Clicks "Try neatlogs free" (leads) | 0 | 4 lost (100%) |

Two different leaks, and I can't yet say which dominates:
1. **Source → listing: 62 → 4.** 93.5% of arriving traffic never reaches the product page. With only 4 views, I can't tell if this is a navigation/positioning problem or just direct traffic that isn't really shopping.
2. **Listing → click: 0 of 4.** A 0% click rate on 4 views is statistically indistinguishable from normal early-stage flop. **Too little data to tell** whether the headline/CTA is the issue — 4 views can't support a conclusion either way.

**What I'd need to know:** why all 62 visits are "direct" while 3 published blog posts logged **zero** tracked visits. Either the posts aren't driving anyone, or their links aren't tracked. Without resolving that, the blog channel is invisible in the data and I can't attribute anything.

## Recommendations

1. **Content — publish the 4 X drafts and stand up tracked links.** An entire planned channel is sitting in draft; publish one variant of the "agent failed in prod" angle with a UTM-tagged link so it shows up as its own source rather than being swallowed by "direct." Right now X, blog and referrer are all at exactly 0 visits, which is a tracking/coverage problem before it's a copy problem.
2. **Content — don't tune the headline yet; fix traffic volume first.** With 4 listing views I cannot responsibly A/B a headline. Get listing views to ~50+ (via the X + blog links above) before judging the click-through rate, then test one headline variable at a time.

I did not pull competitor data — this question is about our own funnel numbers, so Crustdata credits weren't needed.
done|**Crustdata data (neatlogs + 3 competitors, called once, all 4 returned; note web_traffic and competitors_per_crustdata were empty for every company — so this rests on descriptions + headcount/funding only, not traffic):**

| | neatlogs | Langfuse | LangChain/LangSmith | Braintrust |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Founded | 2025 | 2022 | 2022 | 2023 |
| Employees | 11 | 26 | 429 | 169 |
| Funding | none listed | $4M (seed) | $160M (Series B, Oct-25) | $121M (Series B) |

**The one honest, verifiable difference worth claiming**

neatlogs' own description is the gap-closer: *"closing the gap between developers and domain experts… instead of vague feedback in spreadsheets, teams collaborate directly on agent traces."* That maps exactly onto "find and fix a failing run": finding is a tracing feature everyone has, but the fix usually needs a domain expert (support lead, ops, clinician) to say what "correct" looked like on that run. neatlogs' claim should be **"your domain experts work the failing trace with you, in the trace"** — a claim about neatlogs, verifiable on its own product.

**Headline options (both about neatlogs only, no competitor names):**
1. "Find the failing run. Then get the person who knows the right answer into the same trace."
2. "Debug production agents with your domain experts, not a spreadsheet."

**Positioning note for Content (internal, from Crustdata, do not publish):** the three named competitors are funded and sized as engineer-facing observability platforms, with the two largest raising at $100M+ and LangChain at 429 staff. That implies their motion is bottom-up engineer adoption at scale. So aim posts at the *small team where the expert is not an engineer* — the pain neatlogs can actually own — rather than at "best tracing tool" comparisons we can't win on volume.

**Caveat:** with 11 employees and no funding/traffic data returned, I'd rather frame this as "the angle to test" than a proven winner. Content tests option 1 vs a generic tracing headline; I'll compare leads per post next run — and I need post-level lead data (not just visits) before I call either one better.

AutoShelf now runs a small B2B store that refers teams to neatlogs. Four agents
(Operator, Analytics, Content, Support) run on OpenRouter models and every run is
traced to neatlogs (workflow → agent → LLM/tool spans, thinking included).
Crustdata powers competitor research; /ops shows each run's steps.

Agent reliability, driven by real traces (each fix has a regression test built
from the run's own token numbers):
- Token grants instead of fixed shares: helpers draw from what the run has left,
  the operator keeps a reserve, and a job too small to finish is refused up front
  (check-in 7 left 18.7k tokens unspent while Content was cut off).
- Last-turn planning from the real next-prompt size; the last turn may make one
  final tool call, then reports. History is trimmed if needed so it still fits.
- Thinking capped per turn by effort, so a turn can't be all reasoning.
- Empty or cut-off replies are retried once, never passed up as "".
- Tools check required inputs and name what's missing.
- Drafts awaiting the owner's approval are visible to the Operator and Content.
- Removed redundant tools (set_price, refund_order, get_ai_spend); a test pins
  each agent's tool list.
- Test DB is generated from schema.ts so it can't drift.

content.text:
Entire's CLI marks setup commands (`login`, `enable`, `plugin install`) as yours to run, not mine, so please run these three. Type each with the `!` prefix so the output lands here:

1. `! entire login`
2. `! entire enable --agent claude-code --import-history`
   - This hooks Entire into Claude Code, so each commit gets a checkpoint linking it to the session that wrote it.
   - `--import-history` also pulls in the last 30 days of sessions, including tonight's work. Without it, checkpoints only start now.
   - **Note:** session logs are pushed along with `git push`, and agentCrew is public, so these transcripts will be public. Entire redacts secrets first, and the judges want this as evidence. If you'd rather keep logs private, add `--skip-push-sessions`.
3. `! entire plugin install graph`
   - This is "entire-graph", the code-relationship map the rules name next to Checkpoints.

Once those are done, I'll do the following:
- **Graph:** build the code graph and use it to check what each change affects before the next fix (the spend-limit guard).
- **Checkpoints:** commit through Entire so the commit carries its checkpoint, then confirm it with `entire checkpoint` and `entire why` on a line I changed.
- **Evidence doc:** write `docs/ENTIRE.md` with the checkpoint IDs, graph output, and a `why` example, ready for the submission.

content.content:
entire graph adds a deterministic, no-egress code graph to Entire checkpoints.

Usage:
  entire graph <command> [flags]

Set up your agent:
  init-agents      Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
  agent-guide      Print the coding-agent operating guide
  index            Build/warm a committed-tree cache variant for matching queries
  capabilities     List parsed languages, relation types, and features

Inspect the graph:
  search           Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)
  neighbors        Who calls this / what does it call (targeted relations)
  impact           One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol
  def              What a name IS: declaration, fields, and method surface
  explain          Resolve symbols named by a failing build or test
  symbols          Stream every symbol definition (bulk NDJSON)
  edges            Stream every relation (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot         Stream the whole graph: files, symbols, and relations (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot-query   Query a compact snapshot without rebuilding the graph

Analyze changes & more:
  commit           Entity-level change list for a commit vs its first parent
  diff             Entity-level change list between two refs
  checkpoint       Analyze the commit behind an Entire-Checkpoint trailer
  verify           Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output
  stats            Human report: graph usage vs grep/read, and estimated token savings

Help & diagnostics:
  help             Show this command listing
  doctor           Diagnose the environment and confirm no-egress
  version          Print the plugin version (and provider name with --json)

Use "entire graph <command> --help" for details on a command.
For coding agents: run "entire graph agent-guide" or "entire graph init-agents".

# How agentCrew uses Entire

Entire gives the coding agent (Claude Code) repository context in two ways:
**Checkpoints**, which save the session behind each change, and **entire-graph**,
which maps how the code is connected. Both are part of how this repo is built.

## Setup

```sh
entire login
entire enable --agent claude-code --import-history   # hooks + last 30 days of sessions
entire plugin install graph                          # entire-graph v0.4.0
entire graph init-agents --repo .                    # writes the graph guide into AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md
```

`entire status` → `Enabled · branch main · Agents · Claude Code · Checkpoints sync to: origin`.
47 checkpoints on `main`, including imported sessions from the build so far.

## Checkpoints: every change keeps its why

Each commit made by the coding agent carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that links
it to the session, prompt and transcript that produced it:

```
0a5d854 fix: spend limit stops agents cleanly instead of failing the run
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M4PB8G1C850QM37F8VYCQZQJ

036fe66 chore: enable Entire session tracking for Claude Code
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M4PB8BWJXR3SB0KZVSFR705P
```

Imported checkpoints cover the earlier debugging sessions, where each fix came from
reading an agent's neatlogs trace, e.g. `01M4P8J0DW339X91J9E234BWD9` ("read the next
trace and fix").

Any line can be traced back to the prompt that caused it:

```
$ entire why src/core/budget.ts:36
  Line 36 in src/core/budget.ts
  export function isBudgetStop(err: unknown): err is TokenBudgetExceeded | SpendLimitReached {

  [MX] by Claude Code · claude-opus-5-5 · checkpoint 01M4PB8G1C850QM37F8VYCQZQJ · session 821ba888 · commit 0a5d8547
```

## entire-graph: locate first, check the blast radius, then change

Worked example, the spend-limit fix (`0a5d854`). Check-in 16's operator run was
marked **failed** when the LLM spend guard tripped.

1. **Locate:** `entire graph search --query "LLM spend budget reached stops model calls and fails the agent run"`
   ranked `chat()` in `src/core/model.ts` (where the guard throws) and `runAgent()` in
   `src/core/agent.ts` (where the run is marked failed).
2. **Impact:** `entire graph impact --symbol chat`:
   ```
   Blast radius: 4 callers (2 direct, 2 transitive), 9 callees, 6 type consumers, 5 data flows
   Callers: modelLoop (src/core/agent.ts) · callLlm (src/core/llm.ts)
            runAgent (via modelLoop) · callLlmParsed (via callLlm)
   ```
   Only `modelLoop` needs to treat the limit as a clean stop. For `callLlm`
   (claim verification), a thrown error already becomes a tool error.
3. **Test first:** `tests/spend-guard.test.ts` failed, then passed after the fix. All 71 tests pass.
4. **Verify the change set:** `entire graph checkpoint 01M4PB8G1C850QM37F8VYCQZQJ`:
   ```
   src/core/agent.ts   ~ function modelLoop body changed (1 dependent)
   src/core/budget.ts  + class SpendLimitReached added
                       + function checkSpend added
                       + function isBudgetStop added
   src/core/model.ts   ~ function chat body changed (2 dependents)
   tests/spend-guard.test.ts  + module added
   ```
5. **Real run:** check-in 17 at the limit ended `done` ("Stopped early: LLM budget
   reached…"), not `failed`, and used 0 tokens.

Graph index for this repo: 81 files, 734 symbols, 1,997 relations (CALLS, IMPORTS,
DATA_FLOWS, …), built locally with no network access.

## How the pieces fit

```
neatlogs trace of an agent run ──► failure found (e.g. Content cut off mid-job)
        │
        ▼
entire graph search / impact ──► the code behind it, and what a change would touch
        │
        ▼
failing test from the trace's real numbers ──► fix ──► green
        │
        ▼
commit with Entire-Checkpoint ──► next real run, compared in neatlogs
```
