file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

input.content:
# agentCrew: inputs for the cfo.ai business plan

Every cost number here was **measured** from real agent runs (`pnpm export:cfo` →
`runs/cfo_inputs.json`). Anything marked **assumed** is a planning choice; change it
in `src/eval/export_cfo.ts` and re-run the export.

## The business

agentCrew is a team of AI agents that runs the online sales and marketing work of a small B2B
company. An Operator agent checks in on a schedule, reads the store's state, and gives jobs
to three helpers:
- **Analytics:** sales, traffic and competitors (Crustdata).
- **Content:** listings, blog posts and social drafts, with claims checked against the product.
- **Support:** tickets.

Risky actions, such as publishing social posts or refunds, wait for the owner's approval.

Customers pay a monthly subscription. What they choose is how often the crew checks in.

## Measured unit cost (live, 2026-10-11)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Live check-ins (Operator + helpers) | 13 (1 failed, before the fixes) |
| Model | `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` via OpenRouter |
| **Cost per check-in** | **0.817¢** (OpenRouter `usage.cost`) |
| Tokens per check-in | 34,336 (cap: `RUN_TOKEN_BUDGET`) |
| Model calls per check-in | 10.8 |
| Duration per check-in | 67 s |
| Total model spend for the whole build-and-test period | **$0.106** |

Every check-in's token use is capped by a per-run budget. Spend is capped by
`LLM_BUDGET_CENTS`. So a customer's worst-case model cost is bounded by design, not
just estimated.

## Pricing and gross margin

| Tier | Price/mo | Check-ins/day | Inference/mo | Gross margin | Margin if the model costs 10x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $29 | 4 | $0.98 | 96.6% | 66.2% |
| Growth | $99 | 24 (hourly) | $5.88 | 94.1% | 40.6% |
| Scale | $299 | 96 (every 15 min) | $23.52 | 92.1% | 21.3% |

Prices and check-in frequencies are **assumed**. Inference per month is the measured
cost per check-in × check-ins per day × 30.

## Fixed monthly costs (assumed)

| Item | $/mo |
|---|---|
| Hosting (VM + backups) | 25 |
| Domain + email | 5 |
| Crustdata API (paid plan; currently the free sandbox) | 95, to confirm |
| Observability (neatlogs) | 0, to confirm the plan |
| **Total** | **125** |

To break even on fixed costs takes **5 Starter customers, or 2 on Growth**.

## Runway inputs (to set in cfo.ai)

- **Starting cash:** assumed **$1,000** (bootstrapped, solo founder, no salary in year 1).
- **Customer growth:** assumed 2 new paying customers in month 1, then +3 a month.
- **Mix:** assumed 60% Starter, 35% Growth, 5% Scale.
- **Churn:** assumed 5% a month.
- **Payment fees:** assumed 5% of revenue (merchant of record).

## Honest status

The demo store (which promotes neatlogs, where a "sale" is a click-through lead) had
63 real visits and **0 leads** so far. Social drafts are waiting for the owner's approval,
so nothing has been posted yet. **Revenue is $0.** The plan above is for selling the crew
as a product, not the demo store's own income.

## Prompt to paste into cfo.ai

> Build a 24-month business plan for agentCrew, a B2B SaaS where a team of AI agents runs
> sales and marketing for small companies.
>
> - **Pricing:** Starter $29/mo, Growth $99/mo, Scale $299/mo.
> - **Variable cost (measured):** $0.00817 of AI inference per agent check-in. Starter runs 4 check-ins a day, Growth 24, Scale 96. That is $0.98, $5.88 and $23.52 a month per customer.
> - **Payment fees:** 5% of revenue.
> - **Fixed costs:** $125/month (hosting $25, domain $5, data API $95).
> - **Customers:** start with $1,000 cash, no salaries; 2 new customers in month 1, then +3 a month; 60/35/5% tier mix; 5% monthly churn.

`runs/cfo_inputs.json`). Anything marked **assumed** is a planning choice; change it

## The business

agentCrew is a team of AI agents that runs the online sales and marketing work of a small B2B
company. An Operator agent checks in on a schedule, reads the store's state, and gives jobs
to three helpers:
- **Analytics:** sales, traffic and competitors (Crustdata).
- **Content:** listings, blog posts and social drafts, with claims checked against the product.
- **Support:** tickets.

Risky actions, such as publishing social posts or refunds, wait for the owner's approval.

Customers pay a monthly subscription. What they choose is how often the crew checks in.

## Measured unit cost (live, 2026-10-11)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Live check-ins (Operator + helpers) | 13 (1 failed, before the fixes) |
| Model | `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` via OpenRouter |
| **Cost per check-in** | **0.817¢** (OpenRouter `usage.cost`) |
| Tokens per check-in | 34,336 (cap: `RUN_TOKEN_BUDGET`) |
| Model calls per check-in | 10.8 |
| Duration per check-in | 67 s |
| Total model spend for the whole build-and-test period | **$0.106** |

Every check-in's token use is capped by a per-run budget. Spend is capped by
`LLM_BUDGET_CENTS`. So a customer's worst-case model cost is bounded by design, not
just estimated.

## Pricing and gross margin

| Tier | Price/mo | Check-ins/day | Inference/mo | Gross margin | Margin if the model costs 10x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $29 | 4 | $0.98 | 96.6% | 66.2% |
| Growth | $99 | 24 (hourly) | $5.88 | 94.1% | 40.6% |
| Scale | $299 | 96 (every 15 min) | $23.52 | 92.1% | 21.3% |

Prices and check-in frequencies are **assumed**. Inference per month is the measured
cost per check-in × check-ins per day × 30.

## Fixed monthly costs (assumed)

| Item | $/mo |
|---|---|
| Hosting (VM + backups) | 25 |
| Domain + email | 5 |
| Crustdata API (paid plan; currently the free sandbox) | 95, to confirm |
| Observability (neatlogs) | 0, to confirm the plan |
| **Total** | **125** |

To break even on fixed costs takes **5 Starter customers, or 2 on Growth**.

- **Starting cash:** assumed **$1,000** (bootstrapped, solo founder, no salary in year 1).
- **Customer growth:** assumed 2 new paying customers in month 1, then +3 a month.
- **Mix:** assumed 60% Starter, 35% Growth, 5% Scale.
- **Churn:** assumed 5% a month.
- **Payment fees:** assumed 5% of revenue (merchant of record).

The demo store (which promotes neatlogs, where a "sale" is a click-through lead) had

content.text:
The cfo.ai inputs are written and pushed. On the way I found and fixed a bug: you don't need to raise the spend limit.

**The spend bug:** every model call was rounded up to a full 1¢ before being recorded. A call really costs about 0.08¢. So the spend guard counted $1.40, while OpenRouter had actually charged **$0.106** for the whole build. I wrote a failing test with the real numbers first, then fixed it. Costs are now stored exactly. I also corrected the past cost records in your local DB from the exact per-run costs, after saving a backup to `runs/autoshelf.pre-cost-fix.sqlite`. About $1.29 is left under the current limit, so you can run real agents again with no settings change.

**What I built for cfo.ai:**
- **`pnpm export:cfo`** (rewritten): the old version needed simulation data that no longer exists. It now reads the 13 real check-ins from the DB and writes `runs/cfo_inputs.json`.
- **`docs/CFO_AI_INPUTS.md`**: the business, measured costs, pricing, margins, fixed costs, runway inputs, an honest status, and a ready-to-paste prompt for cfo.ai.

**Measured per check-in:** 0.817¢, 34k tokens, about 11 model calls, 67 s.

| Tier | Price | Check-ins/day | AI cost/mo | Gross margin | If the model costs 10x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $29 | 4 | $0.98 | 96.6% | 66.2% |
| Growth | $99 | 24 | $5.88 | 94.1% | 40.6% |
| Scale | $299 | 96 | $23.52 | 92.1% | 21.3% |

The prices, fixed costs ($125/mo), starting cash ($1,000), growth and churn are my assumptions, marked as such in the doc. Change any of them in `src/eval/export_cfo.ts` and re-run the export. In particular, the $95/mo for Crustdata is a guess; we're on its free sandbox now. The doc also says plainly that the demo store has had 63 visits, 0 leads and $0 revenue.

All 79 tests pass and tsc is clean. Committed as `d1e5c9e` and pushed.

**For you:**
1. Sign up for cfo.ai, paste the prompt from the end of `docs/CFO_AI_INPUTS.md`, then cancel right away in Settings → Billing.
2. Export the plan (PDF or a link) and drop it in `docs/` so I can link it from the README.
3. Approve the 4 drafts with `pnpm approve:all`.

Next I can do a fresh real run for a clean before/after neatlogs comparison, or start the README and demo script.

You are the Analytics & Marketing agent for AutoShelf: the person responsible for maximizing conversions, in any honest way you can.

AutoShelf recommends B2B tools to teams shipping AI agents; right now it sells only **neatlogs**. A conversion is a **lead**: a visitor who clicks through to neatlogs' signup. You answer the Operator's question with numbers.

## What you own
- **The funnel:** visitors → product page → "Try neatlogs free" click. Find where people drop off.
- **Sources and posts:** which channels (x, blog, direct, referrers) and which individual posts bring leads, not just visits.
- **Experiments and feedback loops:** tell Content which headline or angle to test and judge the result next time.
- **Cost:** what the AI team spends, so leads aren't bought at a silly price.
- **The market:** who neatlogs competes with and how they compare (size, growth, funding, traffic), using Crustdata data.

## Tools
- `get_sales_summary`: leads, page visits per live product, plus AI cost.
- `get_traffic_sources`: visits and leads per source.
- `get_post_performance`: visits and leads per X/blog post.
- `get_competitor_profiles`: Crustdata profiles of neatlogs and its competitors (Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, Raindrop, Arize Phoenix, Laminar by default): headcount, growth, funding, web traffic. Costs credits the first time, then cached for a week.
- `find_similar_companies`: Crustdata search for other companies doing agent/LLM observability, to spot competitors we don't know yet.

## Rules
- Look things up; never guess. Money from tools is in cents; report dollars.
- Always state how much data a conclusion rests on. With only a few visits, say "too little data to tell" and suggest what would produce a clearer signal; never dress up noise as a trend.
- Prefer leads over visits: a post with 50 visits and 0 leads is worse than one with 5 visits and 2 leads.
- Don't settle for "good enough". If you can't explain why visitors don't click through, say what you'd need to find out.
- **Competitor research** only when the question needs it (positioning, which audience to target, what angle to take). Call each tool at most once per run.
- Turn competitor data into a *positioning* recommendation for Content, e.g. "the big players target X, so aim posts at teams with Y problem". Say it comes from Crustdata.
- Competitor data is **for internal decisions only**. Never suggest public claims about another company (their features, size or weaknesses). We only verify facts about neatlogs.

## Finish with
What the numbers show (with the sample size), then one or two concrete recommendations, saying which agent should act on each (usually Content).
You are the Operator of AutoShelf, the founder and product manager of a small AI team.

AutoShelf recommends B2B tools to teams shipping AI agents. Right now it sells one product: **neatlogs** (traces, failure detection, root-cause investigations and evals for AI agents). A "sale" is a **lead**: a visitor clicking "Try neatlogs free" from a listing, post or blog post and going to neatlogs' signup page.

## Your job
Like a founder before product/market fit, your job is to find out what makes the right people want neatlogs, then point the team at it. You decide what matters this run and why; the specialists do the work.

Your team (each one is a tool you call):
- **Analytics** (`ask_analytics`): conversions, funnel, which sources and posts bring leads, what the AI is costing, and **competitor research** via Crustdata (how neatlogs compares with Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust and others). Ask it a specific question.
- **Content** (`assign_content`): every public word: the listing, X posts and blog posts. Tell it the audience, the angle and the goal, not the wording.
- **Support** (`run_support`): answers people who wrote in. Good answers turn visitors into advocates.

## How to run a check-in
1. Look first: `get_store_snapshot`, then ask Analytics a pointed question ("which source brought leads, and where do visitors drop off?").
2. Handle waiting people before chasing new ones: if tickets are open, send Support.
3. Pick at most **3 actions**, the ones with the most leverage on leads. Name the number that made you choose each one.
4. When you need a sharper angle for content, ask Analytics how neatlogs is positioned against its competitors, then brief Content with that angle.
5. When data is thin (a handful of visits), say so and choose actions that *teach you something*, like a blog post aimed at one specific audience, rather than pretending a trend exists.
6. Pair the specialists the way a good startup does: Analytics finds the leak, Content writes the fix, Analytics checks whether it worked next run.

## Rules
- Never let "good enough" stand: if you don't know why visitors aren't clicking through, make finding out one of your actions.
- Everything public must be accurate about neatlogs; Content enforces this, don't push it to cut corners.
- Posts awaiting the owner's approval (`posts.awaitingOwnerApproval` in the snapshot) can only be published by the owner. Don't assign them to Content; mention them in your summary so the owner can approve.
- The whole team shares a token budget per run. Each job you hand out gets a fixed token grant. Every helper result reports `tokens.freeForJobs`: plan the rest of the run around it. A result starting with `NOT RUN:` means the job was too big for what's left; nothing ran, so choose a smaller job or wrap up. Don't call the same helper twice for the same thing.

## Finish with
A short summary: what you did, the number behind each action, and what you expect to see next run.

content.text:
I ran the agent team twice: check-in 18, then three fixes based on its trace, then check-in 19 to test them. All three fixes held in the second run. They're committed and pushed as `687fe30`, and all 84 tests pass.

**What check-in 18's trace showed, and what changed in check-in 19:**

| Problem in check-in 18 | Fix | Result in check-in 19 |
|---|---|---|
| **Claims were silently dropped.** Content sent 8 claims to `mark_claims`, including the "Collaboration" claim its whole new angle depended on. The tool skipped the 3 it hadn't seen before and still answered `{updated: 5, failed: []}`. So listing v7 relied on a claim that was never recorded as checked. | New claims are now saved. A new claim marked false then blocks any listing that repeats it. Covered by 2 tests. | `added: 10`; every claim the new listing uses is on record. |
| **Content's report to the Operator was nearly empty.** Its last turn shipped listing v7 and a blog post, but the Operator only got "update_listing ok; publish_blog_post ok", so it spent another call checking what had shipped. | The last turn now passes up each tool's result in short form. Covered by 3 tests. | The Operator received "version 8" and the blog URL directly. Its tool calls went from 5 to 4 and its prompt tokens from 16.9k to 14.7k. |
| **Analytics re-fetched data it didn't need.** Asked about competitors, it also re-ran the 3 funnel tools. | Prompt change: "fetch only what the question needs". This one is a prompt rule, so it's checked by the live run rather than a unit test. | That job made 2 tool calls instead of 5. |

Both check-ins produced real work. Check-in 18 shipped listing v7 and a blog post for fintech ops reviewers. WITH RECURSIVE tree(id) AS (SELECT '$R' UNION ALL SELECT a.id FROM agent_runs a JOIN tree t ON a.parent_id=t.id)
SELECT r.agent, s.seq, s.kind, coalesce(s.tool_name,''), s.is_error, length(s.content), replace(substr(s.content,1,220),char(10),' ')
FROM agent_steps s JOIN agent_runs r ON r.id=s.agent_run_id JOIN tree t ON t.id=r.id WHERE r.agent!='operator' OR s.kind IN ('tool_call','text') ORDER BY s.ts, s.seq;"
